title: Article 243N — Continuance of existing laws and Panchayats

content.overview: Article 243N provides that notwithstanding anything in Part IX, any provision of any law relating to Panchayats in force in a State immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992, which is inconsistent with Part IX, shall continue to be in force until amended or repealed by a competent Legislature or other competent authority or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is earlier. All Panchayats existing immediately before such commencement shall continue until the expiration of their duration unless sooner dissolved by a resolution of the State Legislative Assembly or, where there is a Legislative Council, of each House of the Legislature.
content.glance: Pre-73rd Amendment Panchayat laws inconsistent with Part IX continue max 1 year (or until amended/repealed earlier). Existing Panchayats continue until end of term unless dissolved by State Legislature resolution.
content.study:
Article 243N transitional provisions:
1. Inconsistent existing State Panchayat laws: continue until amended/repealed or **one year** from commencement of the 73rd Amendment, whichever earlier.
2. Existing Panchayats: continue until expiry of duration unless sooner dissolved by resolution of the State Legislative Assembly (or both Houses where there is a Council).

Examination: 1-year sunset for inconsistent laws; existing bodies continue; legislative dissolution option.

Article 243N — Transitional protection after the 73rd Amendment
Article 243N was a transitional bridge following commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992. Inconsistent pre-existing Panchayat laws could continue only until amendment or repeal by a competent authority or expiry of one year from commencement, whichever occurred first. Existing Panchayats were generally allowed to continue until their term expired unless sooner dissolved through the specified legislative resolution. For a present dispute, do not treat Article 243N as a permanent exemption from Part IX: establish the historical commencement date, whether the old provision was inconsistent, and whether it was amended, repealed or displaced by the constitutional deadline.

sections.heading: Transitional rules
sections.body:
1. Inconsistent pre-73rd Amendment Panchayat laws: continue until amended/repealed or 1 year, whichever earlier.
2. Existing Panchayats continue for their duration unless dissolved by State Legislature resolution.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What does Article 243N provide regarding existing laws and Panchayats?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Article 243N provides that any provision of any law relating to Panchayats in force in a State immediately before the commencement of the Seventy-third Amendment which is inconsistent with Part IX shall continue until amended or repealed by a competent authority or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is earlier. All Panchayats existing immediately before such commencement continue until the expiration of their duration unless sooner dissolved by a resolution passed to that effect by the State Legislative Assembly or, where there is a Legislative Council, by each House of the Legislature of the State.

enhancement.definition: Article 243N is a transitional provision in Part IX of the Constitution. It addresses inconsistent pre-existing State laws relating to Panchayats and the continuation of Panchayats that existed immediately before commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Article 243N temporarily preserved qualifying inconsistent pre-existing State Panchayat-law provisions only until they were amended or repealed by a competent Legislature or other competent authority, or until one year after commencement of the 73rd Amendment, whichever occurred earlier. It separately provided for existing Panchayats to continue until their term expired unless sooner dissolved through the specified legislative resolution.

essentialIngredients: The first limb concerns a provision of a law relating to Panchayats that was in force in a State immediately before commencement of the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992.
The provision must be inconsistent with Part IX for the temporary-continuance rule to apply.
The inconsistent provision continued only until amendment or repeal by a competent Legislature or other competent authority, or expiry of one year from commencement, whichever was earlier.
The proviso separately addressed Panchayats existing immediately before commencement and allowed them to continue until the end of their duration.

An existing Panchayat could be dissolved earlier by a resolution passed to that effect by the State Legislative Assembly or, in a State with a Legislative Council, by each House of the State Legislature.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Article 243N is a historical transition rule associated with the introduction of Part IX by the Constitution (Seventy-third Amendment) Act, 1992. Its first limb applies only to a pre-existing State-law provision relating to Panchayats that was in force immediately before commencement and was inconsistent with Part IX. Such a provision could continue temporarily, but only until a competent Legislature or other competent authority amended or repealed it, or until one year from commencement, whichever happened first. The proviso separately protected the tenure of Panchayats already existing immediately before commencement: they continued until their duration expired unless dissolved earlier by the specified legislative resolution. For present-day analysis, Article 243N should not be treated as a continuing exemption from Part IX. Identify the historical law, its inconsistency, the commencement date, any amendment or repeal, and—if tenure is disputed—the applicable duration and legislative resolution. The official Constitution text states these two distinct transitional rules.
examples: Hypothetical: A researcher examines a State Panchayat-law provision that was in force immediately before commencement of the 73rd Amendment and appears inconsistent with Part IX. The researcher should identify the exact provision and determine whether it was amended or repealed before the one-year outer limit; the provision cannot be assumed to have remained protected indefinitely.

Hypothetical: A Panchayat existed immediately before commencement of the 73rd Amendment and a dispute concerns whether it could continue. The analysis should establish its applicable duration and whether the State Legislative Assembly—or both Houses in a State with a Legislative Council—passed the resolution contemplated by the proviso.
distinctions: Article 243N and a permanent exception: Article 243N is transitional; it does not create a permanent exemption from Part IX for inconsistent State Panchayat laws.

Existing law versus existing Panchayat: the first limb concerns inconsistent provisions of pre-existing law and its limited continuation; the proviso concerns the tenure of Panchayats already in existence at commencement.

Earlier event versus one-year outer limit: the inconsistent provision ceased to receive Article 243N's temporary protection when amended or repealed by a competent authority, or at the one-year limit, whichever occurred first.
Continuation versus early dissolution: an existing Panchayat generally continued until its duration expired, subject to the specific early-dissolution resolution described in the proviso.
problemApplication: Issue: Is a pre-existing State Panchayat-law provision or Panchayat tenure protected by Article 243N?
Rule: Read the two limbs separately—the limited continuation of inconsistent pre-existing law and the transitional continuation of Panchayats existing immediately before commencement.

Application to a law: establish that the provision related to Panchayats, was in force immediately before commencement, and was inconsistent with Part IX; then establish the amendment/repeal date and calculate the one-year outer limit from the legally applicable commencement date.
Application to a Panchayat: establish that the Panchayat existed immediately before commencement, determine its duration, and check whether the prescribed legislative resolution dissolved it earlier.
Conclusion: give a conclusion only on the basis of the identified State law, dates, and legislative records; do not treat the transition rule as indefinite.
